description.en: The arms apart circular toe touch is a dynamic stretch that flows the arms wide and down to the toes. The circular path opens the chest, hamstrings, and lower back in one fluid motion.

en: Stand tall with feet shoulder width apart and arms reaching out wide.
Inhale and reach the arms up and overhead in a wide arc.
Begin to hinge forward at the hips while the arms travel wide.
Bring the arms down and across as the hands reach toward the toes.
Touch the toes or shins at the bottom of the bend.
Reverse the path by sweeping the arms back wide and overhead.
Stand back up tall with arms reaching wide again.
Repeat the circular flow for the full set.
Stretches the hamstrings and lower back.
Opens the chest and shoulders through wide arm reach.
Improves spinal mobility through flexion and extension.
Acts as a dynamic warm up before lifting.
No equipment needed.
Loosens up the entire posterior chain.

description.en: The band alternating biceps curl is performed standing on a resistance band, gripping each end and curling one arm at a time. The bands provide constant tension that increases as the band stretches, building bicep strength with progressive resistance. The alternating pattern increases time under tension on each side.

en: Stand on the middle of a resistance band with feet shoulder-width apart.
Grip the band ends in each hand with palms facing forward.
Allow the bands to be taut at thigh level.
Brace your core and pin your elbows against your sides.
Curl the right band end up by bending only at the elbow.
Squeeze the bicep at the top of the curl.
Lower the band back down with control to thigh level.
Repeat with the left arm. Alternate sides each rep.
Constant band tension through the range
Resistance increases as the band stretches
Single-arm pattern corrects imbalances
Strong forearm engagement
Useful for home training
Easy to scale by changing band tension

description.en: The band decline sit up adds resistance to the decline sit up by holding a resistance band anchored to the floor below the bench. As you sit up, you pull against the band tension, increasing ab loading. The combination of decline angle and band tension makes for a strong loaded ab exercise.

en: Anchor a resistance band to the floor below a decline bench.
Set a bench to a decline angle and secure your feet on the foot pads.
Lie back and grip the band ends at chest level.
Brace your abs hard.
Sit up by curling your torso up against the band tension.
Continue until your torso is upright.
Squeeze the abs at the top.
Lower yourself back down to the bench with control.
Loaded decline sit up
Constant band tension
Builds ab strength with progressive overload
Decline angle extends range of motion
Easy to scale by changing band tension
Useful for ab specialization

description.en: The bar band bent over row combines a barbell with resistance bands to create accommodating resistance. The bands grow heavier as the bar rises, hammering the back at lockout where bar weight alone is easiest.

en: Loop a resistance band around the center of a barbell.
Anchor both ends of the band under your feet.
Stand with feet shoulder width apart over the bar.
Hinge at the hips with a flat back and grip the bar overhand.
Brace the core and unrack the bar slightly.
Pull the bar up toward your lower abdomen by driving the elbows back.
Squeeze the back hard at the top of the row.
Lower the bar slowly back to full arm extension and repeat.
Adds accommodating band resistance to a barbell row.
Bands grow heavier toward lockout for stronger pulls.
Builds back thickness with mixed loading.
Trains the core to maintain a hinged position.
Develops grip and forearm strength.
Adds variety to standard barbell rows.

description.en: The barbell decline pullover is a pullover performed on a decline bench with a barbell. The decline angle increases the range of motion and lat stretch compared to a flat bench pullover. It targets the lats, chest, and serratus anterior.

en: Set a decline bench to 15 to 30 degrees. Hook your feet under the pads.
Hold a barbell with a shoulder-width grip above your chest, arms extended.
Slowly arc the bar behind your head and toward the floor.
Continue until you feel a deep stretch in your lats and chest.
Pull the bar back over to above your chest using your lats and chest.
Keep a slight bend in your elbows throughout.
Use moderate weight. Aim for 10 to 12 reps.
The decline angle allows a deeper stretch than flat.
Increased range of motion from decline angle
Deeper lat stretch than flat pullover
Targets lats, chest, and serratus
Builds overhead flexibility
Useful for chest and back development
Different angle from standard pullover

description.en: The JM press, named after powerlifter JM Blakley, is a hybrid between a skull crusher and a close-grip bench press. The bar lowers toward the upper chest with the elbows tucked and the triceps doing nearly all the work, allowing heavy loading for direct tricep mass and lockout strength.

en: Lie on a flat bench with feet planted on the floor. Grip the barbell about shoulder-width.
Unrack the bar and hold it over your chest with arms extended.
Lower the bar slowly toward the top of your chest while letting your elbows travel forward.
The bar path should look like a hybrid of a skull crusher and a close-grip press — elbows tuck and forearms angle slightly back.
Stop when the bar is just above your upper chest with elbows pointed forward.
Drive the bar back up by extending your elbows powerfully.
Lock out at the top with arms straight over the chest.
Aim for 6 to 10 reps. Use a spotter — the bar path is unforgiving with heavy loads.
Heavy tricep overload not possible with skull crushers
Builds powerful lockout strength for the bench press
Joint-friendlier than skull crushers for many lifters
Allows progressive overload on the triceps
Direct carryover to competitive bench press
Builds tricep size with compound mechanics

musclesWorked: Triceps brachii (long, lateral, and medial heads)

description.en: The cable standing close press is performed standing facing away from a cable station with a close grip. Pressing the cables forward with a close hand position trains the triceps while the standing position adds core and leg engagement to stabilize the body.

en: Set both cable pulleys to chest height with single handles.
Stand facing away from the cable stack with one handle in each hand.
Hold the handles close together at chest level with palms facing forward.
Step forward to create cable tension.
Brace your core and stand tall.
Press both handles forward until your arms are fully extended.
Bring the handles together at the front of the press.
Squeeze the triceps, then lower the handles back to chest level with control.
Constant cable tension through the range
Targets triceps with close grip
Standing position adds full body engagement
Strong core stabilization demand
Useful for hypertrophy training
Functional pressing pattern

description.en: The cable standing one arm triceps extension is a single-arm overhead extension on cable. The lifter grips a handle behind the head and extends the arm up to lockout. The unilateral setup allows full focus on one tricep at a time and builds size and symmetry.

en: Set the cable to a low position with a single handle.
Stand facing away from the cable stack.
Grip the handle in one hand and bring it up behind the head.
Step forward to take tension on the cable.
Brace your core and keep the chest tall.
Keep the upper arm vertical pointing at the ceiling.
Extend the elbow pressing the handle up overhead.
Lower back behind the head with control. Complete reps and switch sides.
Strong unilateral tricep builder
Constant cable tension
Builds arm symmetry
Trains the long head
Useful arm builder
Strong cable move

description.en: Cross jacks are a jumping jack variation where you cross your arms in front of your body (and your feet at the bottom) instead of bringing arms overhead. The crossover pattern adds chest engagement and a slightly different cardio rhythm than standard jumping jacks.

en: Stand tall with feet hip-width apart and arms extended out to the sides at shoulder height.
Jump and cross your right foot in front of your left while simultaneously crossing your right arm over your left in front of your chest.
Quickly jump back to the starting position with feet hip-width apart and arms out to the sides.
Jump again, this time crossing your left foot in front of your right and your left arm over your right.
Continue alternating which foot and arm crosses on top.
Stay on the balls of your feet. Land softly.
Move at a brisk, rhythmic pace.
Perform 30 to 60 seconds per set.
Combines cardio with chest and shoulder engagement
Different stimulus than standard jumping jacks
Builds coordination
No equipment needed
Engaging variation for cardio circuits
Excellent warm-up

description.en: Downward-Facing Dog (Adho Mukha Svanasana) is one of the most recognizable yoga poses — an inverted V where your hips lift toward the sky and your hands and feet press into the floor. It stretches the hamstrings, calves, and shoulders while strengthening the arms and core. It appears in nearly every yoga sequence as a transition or rest pose.

en: Start on your hands and knees in tabletop position. Hands shoulder-width apart, knees hip-width apart.
Tuck your toes and lift your hips up and back into an inverted V shape.
Press your hands firmly into the floor. Spread your fingers wide.
Straighten your legs as much as comfortable. It is okay to keep a slight bend in the knees.
Press your heels toward the floor — they may not reach.
Lengthen your spine. Push your hips up and back. Your body should form an inverted V.
Let your head hang naturally between your arms. Keep your neck relaxed.
Hold for 5 to 10 breaths. Breathe deeply.
Stretches the hamstrings, calves, and shoulders
Strengthens the arms, shoulders, and core
Decompresses the spine
Improves circulation
Foundational yoga pose
Calming and energizing simultaneously

description.en: The dumbbell lying leg curl is a hamstring isolation exercise performed lying face down on the floor with a dumbbell held between your feet. It is the simplest at-home hamstring curl option, requiring only a dumbbell and floor space.

en: Lie face down on the floor. Place a dumbbell between your feet (held between the arches).
Extend your legs straight. Place your forearms on the floor for stability.
Curl the dumbbell up by bending at the knees. Squeeze your hamstrings.
Continue until your knees are fully bent. Hold for one second.
Lower under control. Keep your hips pressed into the floor.
Repeat for the desired number of reps.
The floor version has less range than a bench version, but is more accessible.
Use a light dumbbell and focus on controlled reps.
Isolates the hamstrings with minimal equipment
Works at home on the floor
Builds hamstring size and strength
No bench required
Useful when no machines are available
Easy to set up

description.en: The dumbbell rear delt raise (also called bent-over rear delt fly) is performed bent forward at the hips with dumbbells hanging straight down. You raise the dumbbells out to the sides with arms slightly bent to isolate the rear delts. It is one of the most effective rear delt isolation exercises.

en: Stand tall holding a light dumbbell in each hand.
Hinge forward at the hips until your torso is roughly parallel to the floor (or to a 45-degree angle for an easier version).
Let the dumbbells hang straight down with palms facing each other and a slight bend in the elbows.
Brace your core. Maintain a flat back.
Raise both dumbbells out to the sides in a wide arc by squeezing your shoulder blades together.
Continue until your arms are parallel to the floor at shoulder height.
Squeeze your rear delts hard at the top.
Lower under control over two seconds. Use light weight — strict form matters more than load.
Isolates the rear delts directly
Builds upper back thickness
Counteracts forward-rounded shoulders
Improves shoulder health
Easy to set up
Useful posture exercise

description.en: The dumbbell reverse hyperextension on bench is a loaded version of the reverse hyper, performed lying face down on a flat bench with a light dumbbell held between the feet. Lifting the legs from a hanging position trains the glutes, hamstrings, and lower back. The dumbbell adds resistance to the bodyweight movement.

en: Lie face down on a flat bench with hips at the edge.
Hold a light dumbbell between your feet, ankles squeezing it tight.
Allow your legs to hang off the edge of the bench.
Grip the bench with both hands above your head for stability.
Brace your core.
Squeeze your glutes to lift the dumbbell up by raising your legs.
Continue until your legs are level with or above your hips.
Lower the legs back down with control to the starting position.
Loaded glute and hamstring work
Decompresses the lower back
Strong posterior chain engagement
Builds glute size with progressive overload
Bench setup makes it accessible
Useful for posterior chain training

description.en: The dumbbell shrug is a single-joint isolation exercise where you hold a dumbbell in each hand at your sides and shrug your shoulders straight up toward your ears. The dumbbell version allows a more natural arm position than the barbell — the dumbbells hang at your sides rather than in front of your thighs — and is easier to set up. It builds the upper traps effectively at home or in the gym.

en: Stand tall with feet hip-width apart, holding a dumbbell in each hand at your sides with palms facing your body.
Pull your shoulders back and brace your core. Keep your arms completely straight.
Shrug your shoulders straight up toward your ears as high as you can. Imagine trying to touch your shoulders to your earlobes.
Keep your arms straight and let the dumbbells rise with your shoulders. Do not bend at the elbows — this is not a row.
Squeeze your traps hard at the top for one to two seconds. Do not roll your shoulders forward or backward.
Lower the dumbbells under control by relaxing your traps and letting your shoulders return to neutral.
Repeat for the desired number of reps. Use heavy weight and strict form for best results.
Use straps for heavy loading if your grip starts to fail before your traps.
Direct upper trapezius isolation
Easier on the wrists and shoulders than barbell shrugs
Independent dumbbells expose and correct left-right imbalances
Allows a longer range of motion than the barbell version
Trains grip and forearm strength heavily
Easy to do at home with one pair of dumbbells

description.en: The dumbbell stiff leg deadlift is a hip-hinge variation performed with a dumbbell in each hand and only a slight bend in the knees throughout the lift. It targets the hamstrings and glutes through a long, loaded stretch, making it one of the most effective accessory exercises for posterior-chain development. It is also more accessible than the barbell version for beginners and home gyms.

en: Stand tall with feet hip-width apart, holding a dumbbell in each hand in front of your thighs with palms facing your body.
Set a slight, fixed bend in your knees and hold it throughout the lift. Do not bend or straighten the knees during the rep.
Brace your core, pull your shoulders back, and lift your chest tall.
Hinge at the hips by pushing your butt straight back. Let the dumbbells slide down the front of your legs.
Lower until you feel a strong stretch in your hamstrings, typically when the dumbbells reach mid-shin. Keep your back flat throughout.
Reverse the movement by driving your hips forward to stand back up. Squeeze your glutes hard at the top.
Stand fully tall but do not lean back at the lockout.
Repeat for the desired number of reps. Focus on feeling the stretch in your hamstrings, not on lifting more weight.
Builds the hamstrings through a long, loaded stretch
Strengthens the glutes and lower back with reduced spinal load vs barbell version
Beginner-friendly entry to hip-hinge training
Excellent accessory for the conventional and Romanian deadlift
Improves hamstring flexibility and hip mobility
Highly portable — works at home with one pair of dumbbells

description.en: The exercise ball body saw is a plank variation that uses a stability ball under the forearms. The lifter rocks the body forward and back in a sawing motion. The motion adds core load and trains anti-extension strength.

en: Place the forearms on a stability ball.
Set the body in a high plank position with feet on the floor.
Set the body in a straight line from head to heels.
Brace your core and keep the back flat.
Rock the ball forward by pushing through the toes.
Stop when the ball is at the elbow level.
Pull the ball back by driving the elbows down.
Continue the sawing motion.
Loads the core
Trains anti-extension
Strong plank variation
Builds the abs
Useful for core size

description.en: The high knees lunge alternates a forward lunge with a high-knee drive coming up from the lunge. The combination keeps the heart rate elevated while building lower body strength. It is a strong choice for circuits and conditioning workouts.

en: Stand tall with feet hip-width apart and arms at your sides.
Step forward with your right leg into a forward lunge.
Lower until your back knee almost touches the floor.
Push off your front foot to drive back to standing.
As you stand, drive your right knee up high toward your chest.
Lower the right leg back down to the starting position.
Step forward with your left leg into a lunge for the next rep.
Continue alternating sides at a steady pace.
Combines strength and cardio
Trains lower body in dynamic patterns
Strong core engagement
Improves balance and coordination
Time-efficient combo movement
No equipment required

description.en: The inverted row with bent knees is the easiest inverted row regression. By bending your knees rather than extending your legs straight, you shorten the lever arm and reduce the percentage of bodyweight you pull. It is ideal for beginners building toward full inverted rows.

en: Set a bar at about hip height. Lie underneath it and grip with an overhand grip.
Bend your knees at 90 degrees with feet flat on the floor.
Pull your chest toward the bar by driving your elbows back.
Squeeze your shoulder blades together at the top.
Lower under control.
The bent knees make this significantly easier than straight-leg rows.
Progress to straight-leg inverted rows as you get stronger.
Aim for 10 to 15 reps.
Easiest inverted row regression
Builds pulling strength for beginners
Shorter lever reduces difficulty
Progresses to straight-leg rows
Minimal equipment needed
Safe and controlled

description.en: The jumping pistol squat is an advanced unilateral plyometric exercise where you perform a pistol squat (single-leg squat to depth) and explosively jump out of the bottom on the same leg. It demands extreme single-leg strength, balance, and explosive power. It is one of the most challenging bodyweight exercises possible.

en: Stand on your right leg with your left leg extended straight in front, parallel to the floor.
Lower into a pistol squat by bending your right knee, keeping your left leg extended forward.
Descend until your right thigh is parallel to the floor or deeper. Your butt should approach your right heel.
From the bottom, explode upward off your right leg, jumping into the air.
Keep your left leg extended forward throughout the jump.
Land softly back on your right leg with a bent knee. Immediately drop into the next pistol squat.
Complete reps on one side, then switch.
This is an elite-level exercise. Master the bodyweight pistol squat first.
Builds elite single-leg power
Develops extreme balance and stability
Trains explosive unilateral strength
Carries over to sprinting and jumping
Impressive bodyweight skill
No equipment needed

description.en: The kettlebell good morning is a posterior chain hinge exercise where you hold a kettlebell at your chest (or behind your neck) and hinge forward at the hips, then return to standing. It is similar to a barbell good morning but uses a kettlebell for at-home accessibility. It builds the hamstrings, glutes, and lower back.

en: Stand tall with feet hip-width apart, holding a kettlebell at your chest with both hands cupped underneath.
Set a slight bend in your knees and lock it in.
Brace your core. Pull your shoulders back.
Hinge forward at the hips by pushing your hips back. Keep your back flat.
Continue hinging until your torso is roughly parallel to the floor (or as low as your hamstring flexibility allows).
Drive your hips forward and squeeze your glutes to return to standing.
Maintain neutral spine throughout — never round your back.
Use moderate weight. The kettlebell adds significant load to the hinge.
Builds the posterior chain
Targets the hamstrings and glutes
Develops lower back strength
Easy to set up at home
Easier on the lower back than barbell good mornings
Builds hinge pattern

description.en: The kettlebell two-arm row is a bent-over row performed with a kettlebell in each hand. You hinge at the hips and row both KBs toward your lower ribs simultaneously. The hanging KB handles demand more grip and forearm engagement than dumbbells.

en: Stand with feet hip-width apart holding a KB in each hand.
Hinge at the hips until your torso is roughly 45 degrees to the floor.
Let the KBs hang with arms extended. Back flat.
Row both KBs toward your lower ribs by driving your elbows back.
Squeeze your shoulder blades together at the top.
Lower under control.
Maintain a flat back throughout.
Use moderate weight. Aim for 10 to 12 reps per set.
Bilateral back loading with kettlebells
KB handles demand extra grip engagement
Builds lats, mid-traps, and rhomboids
Easy to set up
Useful at-home back exercise
Develops hinge posture strength

description.en: The leg raise oblique crunch combines a lying leg raise with a side twist. As the legs raise up toward the ceiling, they twist down to one side, hitting the obliques hard. The combination trains the lower abs and obliques in one efficient ab move.

en: Lie on your back with arms by your sides or under your hips.
Keep your legs together with a slight bend in the knees.
Brace your core and press your lower back into the floor.
Lift both legs up toward the ceiling.
Continue until your hips start to lift off the floor.
Twist your legs together down to one side.
Stop just before your legs touch the floor.
Twist back up to center, then alternate sides on each rep.
Combines lower abs and obliques
Builds lower abdominal strength
Time-efficient ab combo
No equipment required
Strong oblique builder
Useful for waist trimming

description.en: The lying glute stretch is a supine (face-up) stretch where you cross one ankle over the opposite knee and pull both legs toward your chest. It deeply stretches the piriformis, gluteus maximus, and deep hip rotators from a comfortable, supported position on the floor.

en: Lie on your back with both knees bent and feet flat on the floor.
Cross your right ankle over your left knee, resting it just above the kneecap. Flex your right foot.
Reach both hands through the gap between your legs and clasp them behind your left thigh (or on top of your left shin).
Gently pull your left thigh toward your chest. As you pull, your right knee will naturally open outward.
Feel the deep stretch in your right glute and outer hip.
Hold for 20 to 30 seconds. Breathe deeply and relax into the stretch.
Release and switch sides.
Keep your head and shoulders relaxed on the floor throughout.
Deeply stretches the piriformis and glutes
Comfortable supine position allows relaxation
Relieves sciatic tension
Improves hip external rotation
No equipment needed
Gentle enough for daily use

description.en: The mountain climber slide with towel uses sliders or a towel on a smooth floor to remove friction. The result is a smoother and more controlled mountain climber that hammers the core and elevates the heart rate.

en: Place a small towel under each foot on a smooth floor.
Set up in a high plank with the hands under the shoulders.
Brace the core and keep the body in a straight line.
Slide one knee toward the chest by pulling the towel forward.
Slide the leg back to the start position.
Slide the other knee in toward the chest.
Continue alternating sides at a controlled pace.
Repeat for the desired duration or repetitions.
Trains the core and conditions the heart and lungs.
Towels remove friction for smoother reps.
No equipment needed beyond a towel.
Builds plank stability under motion.
Carryover to running and athletic conditioning.
Develops anterior core endurance.

description.en: The neck stretch with hand assisted is a simple stretch for the upper trap and side of the neck. The free hand gently pulls the head sideways for a deeper stretch than passive tilting alone.

en: Sit or stand tall with the shoulders relaxed.
Place one hand on the opposite side of the head.
Let the other arm hang at your side.
Gently pull the head sideways toward the shoulder.
Stop when you feel a stretch on the side of the neck.
Keep the shoulders down and avoid shrugging.
Hold the stretch for the desired duration.
Release and repeat on the other side.
Lengthens the upper traps and side of the neck.
Reduces tension from desk work.
No equipment needed.
Easy to perform anywhere.
Improves neck mobility.
Excellent recovery between training sessions.

description.en: The power sled push is a full-body conditioning exercise where you push a weighted prowler sled across a surface by driving with your legs. It builds quad, glute, and calf strength while providing brutal cardiovascular conditioning with virtually no eccentric loading — meaning it causes minimal muscle soreness. It is one of the best conditioning tools in any gym.

en: Load a prowler sled with the desired weight. Stand behind the sled and grip the high or low handles.
Lean forward into the sled at roughly 45 degrees. Arms straight. Brace your core.
Drive your legs by taking powerful, driving steps. Push through the balls of your feet.
Keep your torso at a consistent forward lean. Do not stand upright.
Drive your knees forward and up with each step. Short, powerful strides work best.
Push the sled for the desired distance (20 to 50 meters) or time.
Rest fully between sets. This is not a pacing exercise — each push should be near-max effort.
Low handles bias a more horizontal push (more leg drive). High handles are more upright (easier).
Builds total-body strength and conditioning simultaneously
Minimal eccentric loading means minimal muscle soreness
One of the best conditioning tools available
Develops quad, glute, and calf strength and endurance
Carries over to sprinting and athletic performance
Can be programmed for power (heavy, short) or conditioning (light, long)

description.en: The rear decline bridge is a glute bridge variation where your feet are elevated on a step, bench, or box while your upper back stays on the floor. The elevation increases the hip extension range of motion, loading the glutes through a greater range than flat floor bridges.

en: Lie on your back on the floor. Place both feet on a step, bench, or box.
Arms at your sides, palms down.
Drive through your heels to thrust your hips up.
The elevated feet create a greater range of motion.
At the top, your body forms a straight line from knees to shoulders.
Squeeze your glutes hard. Hold for one to two seconds.
Lower under control.
Aim for 12 to 20 reps per set.
Greater range of motion from elevated feet
Increased glute demand through extended range
No equipment needed beyond a step
Bodyweight exercise — easy to do at home
Builds glute strength and activation
Useful progression from flat bridges

description.en: The resistance band anti rotation dead bug is an advanced core drill. Holding a band that pulls the body to one side while performing the dead bug motion forces the obliques and deep core to resist rotation throughout each rep.

en: Anchor a resistance band at chest height to one side.
Lie on the back perpendicular to the anchor.
Press the hands together with arms extended toward the ceiling.
Hold the band handles with both hands.
Brace the core and press the lower back into the floor.
Lower one arm overhead while extending the opposite leg.
Resist the band pulling toward the anchor side.
Return to the start and alternate sides each rep.
Trains anti-rotation core strength.
Loads the obliques and deep core.
Builds total core stability.
Useful for athletes.
Improves spinal control.

description.en: The resistance band glute bridge adds a mini band around the thighs (above the knees) to a standard glute bridge. The band provides constant outward tension that activates the gluteus medius simultaneously with the gluteus maximus, making the bridge much more effective for total glute development.

en: Lie on your back with knees bent and feet flat on the floor, hip-width apart.
Place a mini band around your thighs above your knees.
Push your knees outward against the band tension throughout the exercise.
Brace your core. Tuck your pelvis.
Drive through your full feet and lift your hips up off the floor.
Continue lifting until your body forms a straight line from knees to shoulders.
Squeeze your glutes hard at the top. Hold for one to two seconds.
Lower under control. Maintain band tension by pushing knees out throughout.
Activates the gluteus medius along with maximus
Excellent for total glute development
Easy to set up at home
Highly portable
Useful warm-up before squats and deadlifts
Easy to scale by band thickness

description.en: The resistance band upper body dead bug uses a band anchored behind the head to load the dead bug from above. Lowering the arms toward the floor while pressing the lower back into the floor trains anti-extension core strength.

en: Anchor a resistance band overhead behind you.
Lie on the back with the head near the anchor.
Bend the knees and lift the feet to a tabletop position.
Hold the band handles with both arms extended over the chest.
Brace the core and press the lower back into the floor.
Lower the arms overhead toward the floor.
Resist the band pulling the arms back.
Return to the start and continue for the working set.
Trains anti-extension core strength.
Loads the abs hard.
Builds total core control.
Useful for spinal stability.
Improves shoulder mobility.

description.en: The reverse grip pull-up is essentially a chin-up — performing a pull-up with a supinated (underhand) grip. The reverse grip shifts more demand to the biceps compared to the standard overhand pull-up.

en: Grip a pull-up bar with an underhand (supinated) grip, hands shoulder-width apart.
Hang with arms fully extended.
Pull yourself up until your chin clears the bar.
Squeeze your lats and biceps at the top.
Lower under control.
The underhand grip increases bicep involvement.
Aim for 6 to 12 reps.
Often easier than overhand pull-ups due to bicep assist.
Increased bicep involvement from underhand grip
Often easier than overhand pull-ups
Builds back and bicep strength
Full bodyweight pulling exercise
Progressive with added weight
Develops pulling strength

description.en: The roll biceps lying on floor is a self myofascial release drill for the front of the upper arm. Lying face down with a foam roller under the bicep and rolling slowly releases tightness from heavy curling and pulling work.

en: Lie face down on the floor.
Place a foam roller under the front of one upper arm.
Extend the working arm out to the side at shoulder height.
Brace the body on the other forearm.
Keep the working arm relaxed over the roller.
Roll the bicep slowly over the roller.
Pause on tender spots for several breaths.
Cover the full upper arm then switch sides.
Releases the biceps.
Reduces upper arm tightness.
Improves elbow mobility.
Useful after pulling work.
Joint friendly release.

description.en: The roll posterior shoulder lying on floor is a self myofascial release drill for the back of the shoulder. Lying on the side with a foam roller under the rear delt releases tightness in the posterior shoulder and rotator cuff.

en: Lie on one side with a foam roller under the back of the shoulder.
Set the bottom arm extended overhead.
Stack the legs for balance.
Brace the core and keep the body relaxed.
Roll the back of the shoulder slowly over the roller.
Pause on tender spots for several breaths.
Adjust angle to cover the rear delt and infraspinatus.
Continue for the working time then switch sides.
Releases the rear shoulder.
Improves shoulder mobility.
Reduces rotator cuff tightness.
Useful for desk workers.
Joint friendly release.

description.en: The seated chin tuck performs the chin tuck exercise from a seated position — ideal for office workers correcting forward head posture at a desk. The mechanics are identical to the standing chin tuck.

en: Sit upright in a chair. Look straight ahead.
Pull your chin straight back without tilting your head.
Imagine making a double chin.
Hold for 5 to 10 seconds.
Release and relax.
Repeat 10 to 15 times.
Perform throughout the workday every 30 to 60 minutes.
This is the most accessible posture exercise for desk workers.
Corrects forward head posture at a desk
Can be done while sitting at work
Strengthens deep cervical flexors
No equipment needed
Quick and accessible
Prevents neck pain from desk work

description.en: The side bridge with arm leg swing is an advanced side plank variation. Swinging the top arm and leg in opposite directions while holding the side bridge tests anti rotation strength and core stability.

en: Set up in a side plank with elbow under shoulder and feet stacked.
Lift the hips so the body forms a straight line.
Brace the core and keep the bottom side strong.
Lift the top arm and the top leg into the air.
Swing both the arm and leg forward toward each other.
Then swing both back away from the body.
Keep the hips lifted and the core braced through every swing.
Complete all swings on one side then switch sides.
Trains elite obliques and lateral core strength.
Challenges balance through dynamic limb movement.
Builds shoulder stability in the side plank position.
Improves hip mobility through the leg swings.
No equipment needed.
Carryover to athletic balance and rotational sports.

description.en: The single dumbbell decline overhead sit up is a loaded sit up performed on a decline bench with a dumbbell held overhead. The decline angle increases ab demand and the overhead weight challenges shoulder stability.

en: Lie back on a decline bench with feet secured under the pads.
Hold a dumbbell with both hands directly over your chest.
Press the dumbbell up so the arms are straight overhead.
Brace the core and keep the arms locked straight throughout.
Sit up by curling the upper body toward the knees.
Keep the dumbbell tracking straight overhead the whole way up.
Lower back down to the bench with control.
Repeat for the desired number of repetitions.
Hammers the abs through the loaded sit up.
Decline angle increases the demand on the core.
Trains shoulder stability with the overhead hold.
Builds full body strength through coordination.
Easy to scale weight up or down.
Carryover to overhead lifting and athletic core.

description.en: The single leg hip thrust is a unilateral glute exercise where you perform a hip thrust with one foot on the floor and the other leg extended in the air. Training one glute at a time exposes left-right imbalances and significantly increases the demand on each working glute compared to two-legged thrusts.

en: Sit with your upper back against a bench and feet flat on the floor.
Lift your right leg off the floor and extend it straight in front of you, parallel to the floor.
Plant your left foot firmly. This is your working leg.
Drive through your left heel and squeeze your left glute to lift your hips.
Continue until your body forms a straight line from your left knee to your shoulders. Keep your right leg lifted.
Squeeze your left glute hard at the top for one to two seconds. Keep hips level — do not let the right side drop.
Lower under control. Complete all reps on the left, then switch.
If too difficult, place the non-working foot lightly on the floor for assistance.
Builds unilateral glute strength
Exposes and corrects left-right imbalances
More challenging than two-legged thrusts at the same bodyweight
Trains anti-rotation core stability
Carries over to single-leg athletic performance
No equipment needed beyond a bench

description.en: The sitting bent over back stretch is a seated forward fold. From a seated position with the legs extended, folding forward stretches the lower back, hamstrings, and calves.

en: Sit on the floor with the legs extended in front.
Flex the feet and engage the quads.
Place the hands on the thighs.
Inhale to lengthen the spine.
Exhale and fold forward from the hips.
Walk the hands toward the feet as far as is comfortable.
Allow the head and neck to relax.
Hold the stretch for the desired duration.
Stretches the lower back and hamstrings.
Calms the mind in classical yoga practice.
No equipment needed.
Improves seated forward fold mobility.
Excellent recovery posture.
Reduces lower back stiffness.

description.en: The sled wide hack squat is performed on a sled-style hack squat machine with feet placed wider than shoulder-width and toes turned out. The wide stance shifts emphasis from the quads to the inner thighs and glutes. It is a strong glute and adductor builder for variety on leg day.

en: Step into the hack squat sled and place your shoulders against the pads.
Position your feet on the platform wider than shoulder-width.
Point your toes slightly out.
Release the safety handles and brace your core.
Lower yourself by bending the knees and sitting your hips back.
Continue down until your thighs are at parallel.
Drive through your heels to stand back up.
Squeeze the glutes hard at the top.
Targets the inner thighs and glutes
Adductor builder
Stable, guided machine path
Easy to load progressively
Reduces lower back strain
Useful for glute development

description.en: The Smith banded full squat combines deep range squats on the Smith machine with resistance bands attached for accommodating resistance. The Smith fixed path eliminates balance demands, the deep range maximizes quad stretch, and the bands force explosive drive out of the bottom while building lockout strength.

en: Set up a Smith machine with bands attached to each end of the bar and anchored low.
Step under the bar and place it across your upper back.
Unrack the bar and step into your squat stance.
Brace your core and squat down through a deep range below parallel.
The bands should be slack at the bottom of the deep squat.
Drive up explosively against the increasing band tension.
Lock out at the top with hips and knees fully extended.
The bands should reach maximum tension at the top.
Deep range maximizes quad development
Accommodating resistance gets harder at lockout
Smith machine fixed path eliminates balance demands
Forces explosive drive
Builds lockout strength
Useful for breaking through squat plateaus

description.en: The smith reverse grip bent over row uses a smith machine with a supinated underhand grip. The grip pulls the elbows tight against the body and biases the lower lats and biceps. The fixed bar path makes it easy to focus on pulling.

en: Set up a smith machine bar at knee height.
Stand facing the bar with feet shoulder width apart.
Grip the bar with an underhand reverse grip at shoulder width.
Unrack the bar and step back.
Hinge forward at the hips with a flat back.
Brace your core and let the bar hang at arms length.
Pull the bar up to the belly button by driving the elbows back.
Squeeze the lats hard. Lower with control.
Strong lat builder
Reverse grip biases lower lats
Trains the biceps
Builds back thickness
Useful back move
Strong machine move

description.en: The staggered leg side bridge is a side plank variation with the top foot placed in front of the bottom foot. The staggered stance widens the base and adds a different load to the obliques. It is a strong oblique builder.

en: Lie on the side with the bottom forearm on the floor.
Stack the bottom leg straight under the body.
Place the top foot in front of the bottom foot on the floor.
Brace your core and keep the body straight.
Lift the hips up off the floor into a side plank.
Squeeze the obliques and glutes hard.
Hold the position for the working set.
Finish then switch sides.
Loads the obliques
Strong side plank variation
Builds the core
Useful for core size
Trains the side abs

description.en: Straight angle pose is a foundational standing yoga stance with a wide leg position and arms extended out to the sides. It is the starting position for many wide-stance yoga poses and serves as a stretch and strength builder for the inner thighs, hips, and core. It often transitions into Triangle, Warrior II, and Wide-Legged Forward Bend.

en: Stand with your feet about three to four feet apart, parallel and toes pointing forward.
Stand tall with your spine long.
Extend both arms straight out to the sides at shoulder height, palms down.
Feel the wide stance through your inner thighs and the arm extension through your shoulders.
Engage your core. Press through the outside edges of both feet.
Hold for 5 to 8 breaths.
Use this position to transition into Triangle Pose, Warrior II, or Wide-Legged Forward Bend.
Maintain even weight distribution between both feet.
Foundational stance for wide-leg yoga poses
Stretches the inner thighs and hips
Builds shoulder endurance
Improves balance and stance awareness
No equipment needed
Easy starting position

description.en: The suspender one arm biceps curl is a unilateral TRX bicep curl. The lifter grips one handle with the working hand and places the other on the hip, then curls the body up using only the bicep. The unilateral pattern builds bicep strength and arm symmetry.

en: Set the suspension trainer at chest height.
Grip one handle with one hand palm facing up.
Place the other hand on the hip.
Walk the feet forward until the body leans back at an angle.
Set the working arm fully extended.
Brace your core and keep the body in a straight line.
Curl the body up by bending the working elbow.
Squeeze the bicep at the top. Lower with control. Switch sides.
Strong unilateral bicep builder
No dumbbells needed
Trains arm symmetry
Builds bicep size
Strong TRX move
Useful arm builder

description.en: The suspender twist uses suspension straps for a leaning rotational core exercise. Holding both handles together with arms extended, you lean back at an angle and rotate the torso side to side against the strap tension. The exercise builds the obliques and rotational core strength.

en: Adjust suspension straps to about chest height.
Grip both handles together with palms facing each other.
Step back to create tension.
Lean back at about a 45 degree angle with arms extended forward.
Brace your core and stay tall.
Rotate your torso to the right by twisting at the core.
Continue until your arms point past your right shoulder.
Rotate back through center to the left side. Continue alternating.
Builds rotational core strength
Strong oblique engagement
Constant strap tension
No equipment beyond straps required
Different stimulus than lying twists
Useful for athletic core work

description.en: The two toe touch is a basic standing forward fold to stretch the posterior chain. The lifter stands with the feet together and bends forward at the hips reaching both hands to both feet. It is a simple stretch for the hamstrings and lower back.

en: Stand tall with the feet together.
Set the arms at the sides and brace lightly.
Hinge forward at the hips with a long spine.
Continue folding forward toward the floor.
Reach both hands toward both feet.
Touch the toes or hold the lower legs.
Hold the stretch and let gravity deepen it.
Roll up slowly to standing one vertebra at a time.
Stretches the hamstrings
Releases the lower back
No equipment needed
Useful cool down move
Easy to do anywhere
Trains hip mobility

description.en: The weighted side crunch adds external load to a standard side crunch by holding a weight plate or dumbbell at your chest or behind your head while performing lateral spinal flexion on the floor. It builds oblique strength and size beyond what bodyweight side crunches can achieve.

en: Lie on your back with knees bent and feet flat. Hold a weight plate or dumbbell at your chest.
Let both knees fall to the left so your lower body is rotated. Your upper body stays flat.
Brace your core.
Crunch straight up, lifting your shoulders off the floor. The rotated leg position emphasizes the right obliques.
Squeeze your obliques at the top.
Lower under control.
Complete reps on this side, then switch legs to the opposite side.
Use moderate weight. Aim for 12 to 15 reps per side.
Adds progressive overload to side crunches
Builds oblique strength and size
Easy to scale by weight selection
Simple execution
No bench needed
Useful for core hypertrophy
